title: Everywhere I look, it's you
takeaway: When you truly love, you start seeing the one you love in everything.
scene: The poet has seen the face of the one he loves, and since that moment nothing else matters. He talks to the beloved, to the moon, and finally to himself. Its moon pictures are also the language of na'at, poems in praise of the Prophet ﷺ.

original: تیرا سوہنا چن جیہا مکھڑا جد دا نظریں آیا اے
لوکی مینوں بھل گئے لوکاں نوں میں بھلایا اے
transliteration: Tera sohna chann jeha mukhra jad da nazreen aaya ae
Loki mainu bhul gaye, lokaan nu main bhulaaya ae
translation: Ever since I saw your lovely moon-like face,
people have forgotten me, and I have forgotten people.
couplets.story: Since he saw the beloved's face, as beautiful as the moon, his whole world has shrunk to that one person. Other people stopped mattering to him. They noticed, and they drifted away.

original: میں ڈٹھا جیہڑے پاسے وی اوسے پاسے نظریں آیا اے
میرے سچے عشق نے ہر تھاں ای تیرے جلوے نوں پایا اے
transliteration: Main ditha jehre paase vi ose paase nazreen aaya ae
Mere sachche ishq ne har thaan ee tere jalwe nu paaya ae
translation: Whichever way I looked, that's where you appeared.
My true love has found your shining beauty in every place.
couplets.story: Now, wherever he looks, he sees the beloved. Because his love is real, he finds traces of that beauty everywhere he turns.

original: میرے ساتھی میرے ساقی میرے محبوب توں آ جا ہُن
تیری یاداں وچ اکھاں نے مینہ رج وسایا اے
transliteration: Mere saathi, mere saaqi, mere mehboob, toon aa ja hun
Teri yaadaan vich akhaan ne meenh raj vasaaya ae
translation: My companion, my saqi, my beloved, come now.
Remembering you, my eyes have poured down rain.
couplets.story: He calls out to the beloved with every name he has: friend, saqi, love. Please come. He has cried so much, missing them, that his eyes have rained like a storm.

original: چناں ایہہ چانی تیری ذرا نئیں جچدی مینوں دے
اوہ چن سہرے اتے جدوں دا نظریں آیا اے
transliteration: Channa, eh chaanni teri zara nahin jachdi mainu de
Oh chann sehre utte jadon da nazreen aaya ae
translation: Moon, your light doesn't please me at all anymore,
not since that other moon appeared to me beneath a wedding veil.
couplets.story: He speaks to the moon in the sky. Your light used to be beautiful, he says, but not now. He has seen a brighter 'moon', the beloved's face under a wedding veil of flowers, and nothing compares. Lovers of the Prophet ﷺ know this picture: a companion once looked from the full moon to him and found him more beautiful.

original: بدنامی دا ڈر رہے تینوں تے مینوں نہ ستایا کر
ایہہ لوکی ویکھ کے آہندے نے توں احمدؔ نوں رلایا اے
transliteration: Badnaami da dar rahe tainu te mainu na sataaya kar
Eh loki vekh ke aakhde ne toon Ahmad nu rulaaya ae
translation: If you're afraid of getting a bad name, then stop tormenting me,
because people who see me say, 'You've made Ahmad cry.'
couplets.story: He ends with a gentle tease. If the beloved is worried about what people think, they should stop hurting him. Everyone who sees his tears already knows who is to blame.

deeper:
Couplet 4 tells the moon that its light no longer pleases him, because 'that other moon' has appeared. Punjabi listeners often hear the Prophet ﷺ here. His companion Jabir described looking at the full moon and then at him, and finding him more beautiful (Tirmidhi). Calling him a moon is one of the oldest ways poets praise him. The poem doesn't name him, so this is a reading, but a natural one.

The second couplet is the heart of a Sufi reading. The Qur'an says, 'Wherever you turn, there is the face of God' (2:115). The lover who sees the Beloved 'whichever way I looked' is describing that experience: once the heart is awake, God's beauty shows through everything. Forgetting people and being forgotten by them is the Sufi idea of turning from the crowd toward God.

The first couplet describes a change in attention. Since he saw that face, he has forgotten people, and people have forgotten him. Sufis call this being so absorbed in God that the rest of the world fades.
why: Anyone who has had a huge crush knows the feeling of seeing that person everywhere. The poem takes that ordinary feeling and points it at something bigger.
prompt: What do you see 'everywhere' when you care about something deeply?
notes: Couplet 4 is the least certain. 'Sehre utte' is read as 'beneath a wedding veil'; it may instead hint that the beloved has married someone else.
